name: Lumbar Radiculopathy
summary: Lumbar nerve-root disorder causing radiating leg pain with possible sensory, motor or reflex changes; distinguish radicular pain from radiculopathy with objective deficit.

looksLike: Leg pain often extending below knee
Back pain may be present or absent
redFlags: Fever, cancer history, infection risk or significant trauma
firstSteps: Screen neurological status and red flags; document baseline strength
Provide education and maintain tolerable activity
Find positions and movements that permit function without repeatedly provoking distal symptoms
selfCare: Track whether symptoms centralize or spread distally

assess: Document baseline dermatomes, myotomes, reflexes and relevant functional strength
Straight-leg raise/slump when relevant; interpret as part of the examination rather than a stand-alone diagnosis
Repeated movement and centralization/peripheralization response without repeatedly provoking distal symptoms
Walking and sitting tolerance, sleep and meaningful activity restrictions
Screen for cauda equina symptoms, progressive motor deficit, severe bilateral neurological symptoms and suspected serious pathology
Check whether findings fit a nerve-root pattern and consider peripheral nerve, hip and other differential diagnoses

tests.name: Straight Leg Raise (SLR)
tests.purpose: Assess reproduction of familiar radicular symptoms and neural mechanosensitivity; not a stand-alone diagnosis.
tests.positive: Familiar radiating leg pain, typically below knee, reproduced in a relevant range; structural differentiation may alter symptoms.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Screen neurological status and red flags; document baseline strength
Provide education and maintain tolerable activity
Find positions and movements that permit function without repeatedly provoking distal symptoms
Coordinate medical review when deficit is significant
dose: Walking in tolerable intervals: 5–10 minutes, repeat as tolerated
Comfortable mobility: 5–10 reps; stop if progressive neurological symptoms occur
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Use directional exercise only when repeated assessment shows a useful response
Introduce neural mobilisation gently when indicated and tolerated
dose: Neural sliders: 1–2 sets of 8–10 gentle reps only if appropriate; avoid aggressive tensioning
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Restore lifting, walking, work and sport capacity
Progress strength and endurance while monitoring neurological status
Plan graded return and recurrence strategies
dose: Progress functional strengthening 2–4 sets of 6–15 reps
Increase walking and lifting demand gradually with symptom/neurological review
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Walking, sitting and work tasks tolerated
Clear escalation plan if weakness or red flags worsen

logic: Confirm nerve-root involvement using the neurological examination and symptom behavior rather than relying only on leg pain.
Track motor deficit carefully. Progressive weakness changes urgency.
Prefer interventions that centralize or reduce distal symptoms.
structures: Lumbar nerve roots, commonly L4, L5 or S1; disc or foraminal pathology may contribute.
mechanism: Disc herniation or degenerative foraminal narrowing
Symptoms may be aggravated by spinal loading, coughing or neural tension
classification: Radiculopathy with myotomal, dermatomal or reflex change
Severity and progression of motor deficit guide urgency
investigations: MRI when severe/progressive deficit, red flags, or persistent symptoms where results will change management.
Urgent referral for cauda equina suspicion or rapidly progressive weakness.
manual: Selected lumbar mobilization may be an adjunct when it improves function.
Neural mobilisation may be considered as part of a broader plan; avoid forceful techniques in progressive deficit.
Gentle lumbar/thoracic mobilization may be used if it improves symptoms.
Traction can be tested briefly; continue only if distal symptoms reduce or centralize.
Avoid aggressive neural tensioning in a highly irritable nerve-root presentation.
modalities: No passive modality reverses nerve-root compression.
Use symptom-relief strategies only as adjuncts; referral and monitoring take priority when deficits progress.
Heat or TENS may be used as short-term adjuncts
Mechanical or manual traction should only be continued when there is a clear favorable response
Heat/TENS can be used for temporary pain control.
No passive modality should delay neurological reassessment or active rehabilitation.
dosing: Directional-preference exercise if present: 5–10 repetitions repeated through the day.
Walking: several short bouts/day, gradually lengthened.
Progress trunk, hip and leg strength to 2–3 sets × 6–15 repetitions when irritability falls.
progression: Progress from symptom-centralizing motion to strength and endurance
Advance neural loading only after irritability decreases
Progress when leg symptoms are less distal, neurological findings are stable and walking tolerance improves.
Build from basic movement to loaded lifting and work tasks.
Increase neural loading only after symptoms stop flaring easily.
mistakes: Calling every radiating pain radiculopathy without neurological assessment
Ignoring progressive weakness or cauda equina symptoms
Treating MRI findings rather than the clinical presentation
Treating all sciatica with hamstring stretching.
pearls: Radicular pain and radiculopathy are related but not interchangeable terms.
Repeatedly document motor function when weakness is reported.
education: Explain that leg symptoms can change before back pain fully resolves.
Teach emergency symptoms: saddle numbness, bladder/bowel dysfunction or rapidly worsening weakness.
Encourage activity within symptom limits rather than prolonged bed rest.
escalation: Urgent medical/surgical assessment for cauda equina or progressive motor loss
Medical review for severe persistent radicular pain with neurological impairment

tests.name: Straight Leg Raise (SLR)
tests.purpose: Assess reproduction of familiar radicular symptoms and neural mechanosensitivity; not a stand-alone diagnosis.
tests.positive: Familiar radiating leg pain, typically below knee, reproduced in a relevant range; structural differentiation may alter symptoms.
tests.patientPosition: Supine; slowly raise the symptomatic leg with knee extended, noting angle and symptom distribution.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Interpret with neurological findings and history; hamstring stretch or back pain alone is not a positive radicular response.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
